utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, where were we? Yes. We were in the middle of

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skiljevic. I understand from your evidence so far, and correct me if I'm wrong, that it is your position that there were no non-Serb civilians detained in Kula prison except for the Muslim civilians from the Rogatica area who were there in 1994 and into early 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some civilians, a small number of civilians. They were the ones who had fled into our territory, that was how the military authorities had formulated that. In practice they had crossed over into our territory. Some of them had just strayed and then they were kept before triage so that intelligence would be gathered from them until they were sent to their territory, and then the majority of cases it was the exchange commissions that sent them there. They released them not to exchange them for others but just to set them free, to release them for security reasons only.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 24211, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The document that's going to come up on your screen, Mr. Skiljevic, is one of the two documents - I see you have it in front of you - that I asked you to look at while we were breaking, and I'd now like to ask you a few questions about it. This is another of the documents that the Prosecution copied at Kula prison in 2003. And this, I take it, is a notebook that records daily events at Kula prison between the 3rd of January, 1993, and the 3rd of November, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And these records would have been kept by your prison staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was the security service that kept them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the English and page 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told, Ms. Gustafson, that English translation has not been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'll look into that. It was when I had looked at it before. I'll just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's showing "denied" on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I will just try to re-release it and see if that works. It should be working now. Well, Your Honours, it should be working as far as our system is concerned. We are going to print it and try to use it on the ELMO instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we proceed with B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, page -- we are at page 18 of the B/C/S. At the bottom of that page it says received at the detention facility as per military command, Mirjana Ugljesic and Fatima Bajramovic. Now, these were two non-Serb female detainees brought in by the military authorities; right? It might be easier if you just look at the screen rather than trying to find the page in the hard copy. As these records state, Mirjana Ugljesic and Fatima Bajramovic, those were two non-Serb female detainees brought in by the military; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mirjana Ugljesic is of Serbian ethnicity. She was in the detention unit and proceedings were conducted with regard to her, and she remained in the KP Dom later on because she was convicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Fatima Bajramovic, she was a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In our prison, Kula, there were four convicted women of Muslim ethnicity and three convicted women of Croatian ethnicity who were transferred to our institution when the women's department of the KP Dom in Foca was closed down. They had all been convicted to long sentences, ranging between ten and 14 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page -- sorry, 81 of the B/C/S. If you look at the top of the page, the top third of the page, this entry indicates that military police from Foca brought five Muslims for exchange: Two older men, born in 1930 and 1937, and three teenage girls, born in 1977 and 1978. And they were brought by the military policeman Zoran Samardzic. Now in your statement at paragraph 43, you referred to the report -- sorry, this is an entry for 21st of March, 1993. You referred to the duty officer report for the 21st and 22nd of March, 1993, in your statement at paragraph 43; that document is D3357. And that document also states that five Muslims were brought from Foca for the purpose of an exchange, scheduled for the 23rd of March, 1993. Now, the two documents are referring to the same group of people, right, because they both state that there are five Muslim prisoners, they both state that they are from Foca, and they both state that they are being brought in for exchange on this date; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons who had been taken prisoner and were held at the Foca prison were brought to our institution on several occasions. Whether it was this group that arrived then or if it was another one but I remember quite well that on the 21st of March, these persons were brought, had spent the night in our institution, and then the following day they were taken for exchange to the airport by the exchange commission. Sometimes they were brought in larger groups, but only to be exchanged. Some of them stayed for a day, some for a longer period such as one month or more. They would stay at the KP Dom until the exchange was completely arranged.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the English is now available, so if you give us the page number we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, we are now at page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, in your statement at paragraph 43, referencing the duty officer report for this same day that noted the detention of these five prisoners, you said that this shows that POWs in the Butmir KPD were exchanged for Serb captives held in Muslim camps. Now you must have known that these three teenage girls and two older men were not POWs, they were Muslim civilians who were being detained and then exchanged; right? You must have known that.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As the prison warden, it's not true that I must have known that. It was not a description of my duties. They were the ones who did it, the military security, the security organ, that is to say, and the exchange commission. They were in charge of that and they took them to be exchanged. I did not hold talks with the commission president. Amor Masovic, for example, I never even met him, nor did I make lists or go to meetings with SFOR and other international organisations, such as the ICRC and so on, to compile lists and decide who would be exchanged and who wouldn't and who was a civilian and who was a POW.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back into private session again momentarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, one more question on this topic before we move on, you've given me very formalistic answers about jurisdiction and authority, but you were the prison warden at the time. You saw these people coming and going, people like the teenage girls we just saw. I would think that any thinking human being would question this entire process of detention and exchange and whether it was about prisoners of war, as you're asserting, or whether this was just about getting Muslims and Croats out. Didn't those questions ever cross your mind when you saw the kinds of people being detained and exchanged at your prison?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did think along those lines. And perhaps over time I might publish a book about Kula and Kula as a prison, but as someone who was head of the institution appointed on 16th of December, 1993, when I took over the duties and the POW unit which had been formed earlier, it wasn't formed by the Ministry of Justice, that is to say the civilian authorities, but rather the Ministry of Defence. The rules and the instructions have been signed by Bogdan Subotic, general and minister of defence rather the minister of justice, Momcilo Mandic or Jovo Rosic, who was my superior as the minister. So if I mentioned the example that the minister personally came to visit the prison - that was Mr. Rosic - and he did not want to visit, just the detainees, the civilians, and the detainees, only those who were under the jurisdiction of the district court, and that I as the warden needed to inform him that there were others there as well, but they didn't want to discuss that at all. And at our meetings of the collegium of the ministry, we would inform them about the problems that we as the wardens had with various categories that were brought to the KP Dom. We had had enough even of the Serbs who were being brought. Those were the reasons why we didn't get involved into any analyses and we didn't look into those persons' files, we didn't use psychologists or other professional staff to work with such people because according to our plans, our authority, our jurisdiction we were not allowed to do that. Privately I could talk with anyone if I wanted to collect some information, but not nor official purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify something in your answer, you mentioned visits by the minister of justice, Mr. Rosic, and you said: "... I as the warden needed to inform him that there were others there as well, but they didn't want to discuss that at all." Are you stating there that you were -- you informed the minister of justice of your concerns about civilians being held in the prison but he didn't want to discuss that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At meetings we also pointed out that we had major problems, the problem was not that they were accommodated there but how to food them and providing heating, provide health care, all sorts of problems, and we had this burden. We had to see how to do it via other organs, and everybody else was saying that they were not under our jurisdiction and that we wouldn't be involved. We shouldn't release them, we shouldn't make any impact on the exchange or anything along those lines, but just that we should work in a decent and professional manner, as in 1992, the president, Mr. Karadzic, also told us at the very beginning of all these developments when he came to visit us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the civilians from Rogatica for a moment. In your interview with the Prosecution in 2003, you said from 1993 and on to 1994 civilians would come - the area around Sokolac or Rogatica, for example - as so to say humanitarian cases where it was said that they would stay for a short period of time, that only the deal about the exchange is being awaited and they would stay for a month or two waiting for the transfer. Now, that's right, isn't it? The civilians from Rogatica were being held at Kula while the deal about their exchange was being arranged?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I must say that we didn't want to receive those civilians. We were actually tricked, the management of the KPD, because the buses arrived without notice. We did have separate facilities so that these people are not mixed, do not mix with the others, but we received them anyway because we felt pity for them. And they would stay for five, ten, 15 days, as long as it took for the UNHCR or the ICRC to arrange everything for those people to go to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said five, 10 or 15 days but the document you reference in your -- sir, the document you reference at paragraphs 19 and 38, which is D3335, states -- is dated the 5th of September, 1994. And it says the problem, lack of funding for food, et cetera, has been particularly prominent in the last three months when a number of refugees from the Rogatica municipality were accommodated in the prison, mainly women and underage persons. So by the time you wrote the letter on the 5th of September, 1994, at least some of these prisoners had been there for three months; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends from where they had come because there were people who came from one village and most of them leave and then people from another village arrive. It's true that I wrote a letter to ask for assistance from the government and the high commissioner's office, and I always asked for assistance in advance, to avoid a situation in which I would be unable to feed the people, and that indeed never happened. There was also a problem with electricity. We needed candles and all sorts of stuff.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because we are moving now away from the question which was just about the time period. And if I could ask you again to try to focus your answers as much as possible on the specific question. Now, I am going to mover on to another topic. I will come back to this document on the screen later so I won't tender it at the moment. At paragraph 6 of your statement you said that prisoners occasionally went out to work on the orders of the military. At paragraph 7 you said you did not know what kind of labour these people were taken to do. And then at paragraph 51 you said as far as I know such work was generally carried out in the depth of the territories. Now, your own documents, the ones that are attached to your statement show that you in fact had detailed information about the kind of labour these prisoners did and that it was often carried out at front line positions. So, for example, D3352 that you reference at paragraph 51 is a military request to Kula prison asking for 15 prisoners who will be tasked with building trenches and communication trenches in Donji Kotorac; that's page 6 of D3352. Similarly, page 9, another military request, asks for 15 prisoners who will work on building trenches and communication trenches near Kuca Novakovica, and Donji Kotorac. These requests indicate that you were basically informed exactly what kind of work these prisoners were going to do and where; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two examples you have read out, the locality is the site of the KPD, Donji Kotorac and Kuca Novakovica. It was the -- the works were about the roads.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, could you repeat your answer. Interpreters couldn't hear you. If you could kindly repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two letters, Donji Kotorac and Novakovici, they border on our land, the Privrednik unit. Behind that, there is the Sarajevo airport. Of course, I'm always well acquainted with this locality. But other places, for example, when they were being taken to the barracks for labour, we didn't know what kind of work they had to perform there, whether they would chop wood or work in a kitchen or repair roads. We were only able to get feedback after inquiring. Sometimes they would remain at the barracks for a month without returning to the KPD. It would also happen that an exchange commission arrived but the people were physically absent, they were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We will have Exhibit P5987 referenced at paragraph 52 of your statement. That document informs the Kula prison authorities that a group of Muslim prisoners were building bunkers at Ozrenka Street positions which were constantly under infantry and rifle grenade fire. That's another example of detailed information you received about the nature of the work at a front line position; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information, whether or not the people were at the front line, because our facility was also very near the front line. We were shelled occasionally. So although I'm not a military expert, I know that the barracks -- that barracks were near and the KPD, and the farm, they were all near the front line, and everything needed protection, as well as the roads that went through Lukavica to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 24236, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Skiljevic, this is the other document that I gave to you the other day to look at. It's the one with the number 24236 on the cover. Now, this is the -- again this is a document that the Prosecution received from Kula prison in 2003 and this document records when prisoners went out to work and came back. It's the -- basically the work site list for the period 24 September 1992 to the 2nd of January, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've had a chance to review this. The records in this notebook indicate that groups of Muslim prisoners from Kula were sent out virtually every day during this time period to work at military locations such as Grbavica, the Slavisa Vajner Cica Barracks, Trebevic, Zlatiste, Dobrinja, and the Jewish Cemetery; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you had said at paragraph 50 of your statement that, in general, prisoners of war performed the same work as Serb convicts. Just to clarify, that's only true for the work that was carried out within the prison compound. It was only the non-Serb prisoners who were sent out to work for the military at these military locations; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you've had a chance to look at that notebook. As I read it, the names are listed under all of these military work sites and the names refer exclusively to non-Serb prisoners being sent out to military locations. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 70 per cent right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you during the next break to have a closer look at that notebook. And if you can identify any names of Serbs who were sent out to look at -- sorry, to work at military locations, you can inform the Court of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to now go to 65 ter 24211, which is the same document we were looking at a few moments ago. If we could go to page 4 of the English and page 23 of the B/C/S. And I would tender the document we just looked at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the Defence accept that there is no Serbs that had been sent out to work in military places?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, that's why I think it's good to admit the entire document so if there are such names it can be seen. And, perhaps, I don't know if the witness will actually have a chance to look at that but at least it can be in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on this page, Mr. Skiljevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 24236 will be Exhibit P6280.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, we're back. The document on the screen now is the notebook of daily events at Kula in 1993, the one we were looking at earlier. And on this page, we can see examples of military work sites including the Slavisa Vajner Cica Barracks, number 7; Zlatiste, number 11; and Dobrinja, number 17. And under the remarks column, there are six names of Muslim prisoners and that reference -- that indicates that those six Muslim prisoners were taken to the Dobrinja work site; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, the work site lists in this notebook indicate that during this periods of time, which is 3rd of January, 1993, to the 3rd of November, 1993, Kula prisoners continued to be taken out to military locations to work, more or less on a daily basis; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 13 of the English and page 59 of the B/C/S. This is the entry for the 27th of February, 1993, and we can see that one of the work sites at number 13, towards the bottom of the page, is Sucuri. And if we go to the next page of the English and zoom in on the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, there is a remark here indicating that the persons who worked at the workplace near Sucuri complained that they dare not go to the above mentioned workplace because they have been maltreated and physically beaten. And if we could just go to the next page in the B/C/S, page 61, this is the entry for the 2nd of March, and again it shows Sucuri being one of the work sites at number 13. And the next page in the B/C/S, again Sucuri is one of the work sites listed. It's there at number 14. And I can tell you it is listed again for the following two days. Now, in your statement you said that you knew that none of the prisoners complained about being mistreated while working or while staying at the KP Dom itself. Here your records indicate that prisoners were complaining about being physically mistreated while working at Sucuri. This was recorded in your prison records, and they were nevertheless continued -- they nevertheless continued to be sent there to work; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this case very well. This is a settlement near the barracks, the Cica barracks. There were problems there because large quantities of alcohol were consumed. The people who worked there had been given alcohol. This was not the first time that people returning from work were intoxicated. At our facility, near the poultry farm, there was also a Serbian cemetery, and people would go there to drink. We warned of -- we issued warnings about that but we were not in the position to punish anybody because of that. The only means that we had at our disposal to keep the people to work at our KPD and not sends them out. And among these people there are also psychopaths and alcoholics. We informed the military authorities of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Skiljevic, these prisoners were complaining not about being given alcohol, they were complaining about being maltreated and physically beaten. That was recorded in your prison records, and despite that complaint they continued to be sent to this work site; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't send the same people, we sent other people to that work site. I said that there had been a clash with the soldiers guarding them, and both were -- both sides were drunk, and that's how the problems arose.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I take it from your answers that Sucuri was a military work site and the prisoners that were sent there to work, those were the non-Serb prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to tender the parts of this document that have been translated so all the B/C/S pages that correspond to the English, and I'll be happy to liaise with the Registrar on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will receive them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6281, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skiljevic, I'd like to read you another passage from your Prosecution interview in 2003. And this is at page 153. You said: "Upon the control by the ICRC who were always announced on time, and they come to visit the persons, the prisoners of war, they want to talk to them without the presence of the employees. After they talk to them and distribution of some help, some things that they bring, some clothes, toothpaste, soap, they would come to talk to me. Since I as the head of the institution was interested in what remarks they would have, the remarks would exclusively be for the fact that those persons were being used for military needs, that is for digging of trenches. And my answer was always -- because they never had any other remarks as to our attitude or the attitude of the guard or for the food, so my answer would be, Please, it is not under our jurisdiction, and I would ask you to discuss those issues with military command staff because this institution does not need trenches. We only assign people for farming tasks. And I know for sure that those delegations would leave my office going to the command staff and would talk to them over there." Now, it's right, isn't it? This passage is correct. The ICRC complained directly to you about the fact that Kula prisoners were being used for military work like trench digging and you referred them to the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They spoke to me, and most times when somebody was injured or got killed, they would say that they were very concerned about the safety. It is true that I gave this answer to them but I also told them that we had our orders and that they had to go to the military command at the barracks and speak to the people in charge. Whether they went there or not, I don't know. I never got any feedback.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in your interview you said: "And I know for sure that those delegations would leave my office going to the command staff and would talk to them over there." Now, which command staff were you referring to? Was that the SRK command, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in 2003 you were sure, or you said you were sure that they would speak to the command staff. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they told me that they would go to the command to talk. But I didn't go with to see whether they really had gone there. I said where they had to go but they knew anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, could we have 65 ter 24190, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The document that's about to come up is another document that the Prosecution copied at Kula prison in 2003. And it's an RS central exchange commission document titled "information on wanted persons." And it appears from the contents to be persons wanted by the Muslim side, prisoners wanted by the Muslim side. If we could go to page 6 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. There are a number of entries in this document. I'd like to look at entry 8 which is right in the middle of the B/C/S and near the bottom of the English. This is the entry for Samir Hidic. And it has different pieces of information from different dates, and there is one right around the middle of the paragraph and this is right at the bottom of the page in the English. It says, "25 November 1993." The information for that date says, "According to report received from KPD Butmir." Sorry, if we go to the next page of the English: "According to report received KPD Butmir they were killed by a shell on Zlatiste. Even ICRC decried Serbian side for forcing prisoners to work on the first line." I think that should be front line. And then the next entry says: "23rd of March, 1994, according to reports received from Soniboje Skiljevic, there is no new information." And there is a similar entry if we go to page 5 of the B/C/S and page 9 of the English. This is the entry for Mustafa Hrtic, number 11, so it's in the -- it's the second entry in the B/C/S. And again, for the 25th of November, 1993, it says: "According to KPD Butmir he was killed by a shell on Zlatiste. ICRC decried Serbian side for forcing prisoners to work on the front line." And then again, it says for the 23rd of March, 1994, according to reports received from you, there is no new information. Now, the -- this document shows that the Kula prison authorities informed the central RS exchange commission of the fact that Muslim prisoners were working at front line positions and that the ICRC was protesting this practice; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exchange commission and the commission president knew of that. Because we see that the exchange commission was notified at the airport. The representative of the exchange commission for the people who were from Grapska is from the 1st Krajina Corps. I only gave him accurate information in case a list came in, a list of people about which he would brief the others at meetings. There was no intention of concealing an individual or saying that he was there in order to hide the fact that the individual had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I realise as we went that I had an earlier translation. The translation I have says "information on wanted persons," but I'd have to look at the screen again to see if that has been revised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, I'd like to read another passage from your interview in 2003 on this topic. You were asked -- this is at page 158. You were asked: "I have to go back. Again in 1992, you mentioned that you would report to Avlijas. Would that be in writing or verbally?" And you said: "More verbally and some in writing. As I've said he would come here very often and that he was familiar with the problems of all KP Doms, once he assumed the position of assistant for implementation. And issues most often discussed were the issues on prison regulations, passing the house rules, law on implementation of criminal and misdemeanour sanctions, systematisation of work positions, resources needed for the institutions, equipment level of the police service." And then you were asked: "Thank you. Would you also inform him about the fact that the work done by the prisoners?" And you said: "Yes, he was familiar with that." And you were asked: "And what was his reaction to the fact that prisoners would be taken and would be used for military purposes?" And you said: "I think he had contact with them and talked to them. I think I said that in the beginning -- I think I said that in the beginning what was the answer, that we had none, nor we could -- nor could we have had any influence, that is that anybody could have prevented it, any of us could have forbidden it." Now, that's right, isn't it? You -- as you told the OTP you were in constant contact with Slobodan Avlijas, the assistant minister of justice who came to Kula very often, and he was aware that Kula prisoners were taken out to do military work and his response was that he was unable to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions, Mr. Avlijas, the assistant deputy minister, every time I was there would come. He would tour the institution. We went to meetings in Bijeljina with him because the implementation was in Bijeljina. The only person for the implementation of sentencing. He would call several times, he would come -- he would frequently say, Are you alive, take care of yourself, because everybody knew where we were and in which area of the war we were. It's true that the minister was informed as well as the assistant about all of the problems because this is our job, anything that had to do with convicted persons, something that was in the jurisdiction of the district courts. But anything that had to do with the military jurisdiction, there were several categories of detainees that we had. And there was also a women's section, plus civilians and prisoners of war, and three warring parties. All of that was something that Mr. Avlijas was aware of. So the answer that I gave then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, the interpreter did not hear what you said after you said, "So the answer that I gave then." Could you finish that sentence again, please?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was in 2003 that I gave, that you read, to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the answer that you gave in 2003 about Mr. Avlijas's knowledge of specifically of prisoners performing -- being taken out to do military work, that's accurate and correct; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 24237, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, the document that will come up on your screen in a moment is a document that the Prosecution copied at the Kula prison in 2003. And it is a report of an inspection of Kula prison that took place in April 1994. And at the bottom it says, "Pale, April 1994." Would this inspection have been carried out by Ministry of Justice officials, Mr. Skiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see the first part here. Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It doesn't have a signature. That's why I'm asking you. Perhaps we can go through it and then it may refresh your memory about the inspection. If we could go to page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. And in the middle of the page, it says, "Conditionally put, three categories of persons are located in the facility." A is 89 persons under investigation. And under B it says 14 convicted persons. And then at the end of the part under B it says 75 Muslim including four women and 46 Croatian prisoners. And if we could go to page 4 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. And this is at the top of the B/C/S, in the middle of the English, it says: "The food is being prepared in the facility's kitchen as follows: For facility employees, employees of the Kula police station and convicted and detained persons of Serbian ethnicity, according to a set menu issued once a month, while different food is prepared for prisoners. Everyone eats in the facility dining room except Muslim prisoners whose food is brought to the rooms they inhabit." Now in your statement you said that the same food was served to the prisoners, guards, and KP Dom officials, but this report indicates that while the Serb convicts and the Serb detainees ate the same food as the prison staff, the non-Serb prisoners were given different food; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report written by the inspector, it's not said here but if the cooking was in the military army cauldrons and then taken to the Muslims, then there was a request; for example, when beans were being cooked, not to put pork into that meal. And then they asked for food to be cooked on oil, not on lard. That would be the main difference. There was a problem with the pates, for example, that we received from the Red Cross produced by Ikar. In that food, perhaps if there was any fat or anything else, a number of them would avoid eating it, not all of them but a number did avoid eating it. And we had to fulfil their requests of the people who were working there, as this inspector here has written in his observations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And although in your statement you said that food was provided to interned persons in the dining room, this document clearly states that Muslim prisoners did not eat in the dining room, they eat in the rooms in which they were imprisoned; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to this, it would seem that they ate in their rooms, but they actually had their own dining room between the two facilities. It was difficult to prepare 1200 meals every day and to issue them at the same time. The people who were going to work had to have breakfast first, then they would have a snack, then they would come for lunch, then it would be officials, we had professors, district courts, police, people from the Ministry of the -- of internal affairs, employees. There was a separate room for that or actually a canteen or a dining room. Food was not taken to the rooms, in any event. Only if somebody was ill perhaps, then it would be taken to them because they couldn't come to the dining hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, having had a chance to see some of this report, do you recall now whether this inspection was carried out by Ministry of Justice officials in April 1994?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was one inspector at the Ministry of Justice at the time, and I think that he wrote this report. The document should have been signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document and I'd like to now go to 65 ter 24232.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6283, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The next document we are going to look at Mr. Skiljevic is actually the appeals judgement by the Bosnian state court, the document that you reference in your statement but is not tendered. And it's referenced at paragraph 17 of your statement. And you noted that you were acquitted on appeal. If we could go to page 74 of the English and page 56 of the B/C/S, and if I could direct your attention to paragraph 194 of the judgement, and this is in the section of the judgement dealing with conditions in the prison between the 16th of December, 1992, and mid-December 1995. And it refers to eight witnesses -- starting in the second sentence who all -- eight witnesses and others, it says, discussed overcrowding in the KPD Butmir. They slept on mattresses and blankets, had insufficient foods which mostly consisted of two meals and endured poor hygienic conditions. And it says some witnesses testified that they had the possibility of bathing with cold water and about the lack of heating during the winter months. And the Court states, these conditions are undoubtedly unsatisfactory, although it notes some witnesses said that the conditions were better than other camps in which they had been detained. And if we could go to paragraph 177 which is on page 70 of the English and page 53 of the B/C/S, at paragraph 177 it states that the Defence teams for both accused agreed that the detention conditions with respect to the provision of food and hygienic accommodation were not satisfactory but argued that the army was responsible for meeting the dietary and hygiene needs of detained non-Serbs. Now, in your statement in this trial, at paragraph 8, you asserted that the food at KPD was sufficient and none of the prisoners went hungry, whereas at your own trial you agreed that the food and other living conditions for non-Serb prisoners at Kula were inadequate and blamed the army for this; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't wish to comment on the judgement of a trial chamber or any court decisions. Simply I would not want to comment on that. This is an official judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You've already commented on this judgement in your witness statement, Mr. Skiljevic. You put it forward in asserting that you were charged with crimes at Kula camp and acquitted. And this states clearly that the position you took in your own trial was that the food provided to the non-Serb prisoners at Kula was inadequate. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It depends on the period that you're talking about. I am talking about the period from 1993. I'm not talking about the initial period. We don't want to mix things up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that I'm at the end of my time. I could conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now just remaining on the topic of this judgement that you point to in your witness statement, I'd like to summarise the reasons for which you and Mr. Lalovic were acquitted and you can tell me if you agree with that. The appellate chamber concluded that Kula prison constituted an organised criminal system in which large numbers of non-Serb civilians were unlawfully detained and provided with inadequate food, hygienic facilities and medical care, and subjected to forced labour resulting in injuries and death. The appellate chamber also concluded that you were undoubtedly aware of this criminal system. But the chamber acquitted you of unlawful detention, inhumane conditions of detention and forced labour because it found there was a reasonable doubt that you, as opposed to the Republika Srpska military authorities, were responsible for those crimes. Do you agree with that summary?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The last sentence was that you were acquitted of unlawful detention, inhumane conditions of detention and forced labour because the appeals chamber found that there was a reasonable doubt that it was you rather than the military authorities of the Republika Srpska that were responsible for those crimes.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we were responsible?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, the appeals chamber concluded that the military authorities may have been responsible for the crimes rather than you, and that's why you were acquitted; right?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's better now, because before you said that we were responsible. I can just give a brief comment. During the war, the Kula KP Dom, and I'm telling this Trial Chamber and all those present, that there was no institution in Republika Srpska or Bosnia-Herzegovina that had better accommodation, food and everything than the KP Dom, and this has been proven in trial proceedings so far. Mr. Mandic, the warden, and the seven wardens and guards who were tried before the court in eastern Sarajevo showed that everything that the Prosecution charged and sought to prove could not be proved against us responsible ones. So far, there have been 11 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, again, do you agree that the appeals chamber found that all these crimes were committed at Kula, unlawful detention, forced labour, cruel treatment, the reason you were acquitted is because the Court concluded that the military authorities may have been responsible for those crimes carried out at Kula prison. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No single crime was committed in Kula, specifically. If there was any crime, it was from a shell that killed Serbian people and a shell that dropped in the military farm and another shell when a policeman on duty was killed. No person was killed in the facility of the KP Dom. Secondly, it's correct that at work sites and during work duty at the farm and outside of the KP Dom, there were some people who were killed and who were wounded. I'm not disputing this and I did not dispute this before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection. I think it should be admitted in its entirety since the reasoning was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Mr. Robinson, has the Chamber ever admitted a judgement of a different chamber or court? If you could remind me of our practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you've been admitting portions of judgements in the past. We have usually taken just the portion that showed the result without the reasoning, but there have been other occasions when you've admitted portions of a judgement either showing someone was convicted or acquitted. In this case we think the whole judgement should be admitted because the questioning dealt with not only the outcome but the reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I might add in the Prosecution's case the Chamber admitted -- I'm aware of at least two full judgements that were admitted by the accused in cross-examination relating to crimes in Rogatica. I don't have the numbers at my fingertips but I could certainly find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take this under advisement and come back to this issue later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, but I see the time, so I'm wondering if we should begin now or would it be better to do it after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 3 minutes to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could just take the opportunity to inform the Court of the exhibit numbers of the judgements you had previously add admitted. They are D1665, and D1666. And if I could just add that apart from that I think these are somewhat unique circumstances given that the judgement I tendered was raised, discussed and referenced at paragraph 17 of the witness statement. And as it's raised in the sense of the witness's acquittal it could leave an impression that the Bosnian state court concluded that crimes weren't committed at Kula, whereas the judgement as a whole makes it quite clear that the Court concluded crimes why systematically committed at Kula prison. So I think to put the assertions at paragraph 17 in their proper context, that these are circumstances where fairness would militate in favour of admitting this exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will consider the issue. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not quite certain that it can be taken that the Court determined responsibility for events in Kula. It determined that this witness and his associates were not guilty. But the Defence will consider this further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Skiljevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us start with what is the freshest. Did the Muslim prisoners provided less food than the Serbian ones?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give less than you had and less than you could to Muslim prisoners and anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did you purposefully withhold food and items needed for personal hygiene, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that for POWs, you requested assistance in food from the army. As for those who were criminally prosecuted, the minister of justice was in charge of them. And how did you treat the Muslim civilians, those who arrived to be exchanged and for your reunification with their families, were they treated as prisoners at all?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were separated from the detainees in another building, so they were not covered by the same treatment in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have sufficient food for them, and how did you arrange this?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the contingent of food that was available for us, and which we produced at our farm, we also requested from the government and the high commissioner to send us certain produce because a group of civilians from the vicinity of Rogatica was accommodated in the Dom so we wouldn't be in the situation if we received more people from other locations, that we would not have sufficient food and we would have hungry people and wouldn't be able to feed them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 24191, please. If we could have that document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your document with your signature and do you remember -- no, no, first page, please. But I think it's not -- what we have now is not -- the previous page, rather. The previous document. Yes, thank you. Can you please answer, is this your document with your signature and who did you address this request to?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed this request on the 5th of September, 1994, to the commission for refugees and humanitarian aid of Republika Srpska in Pale, that is to say the commissariat for refugees and humanitarian aid of Republika Srpska in Pale. All the requests before this one and this one too were fully granted, thanks to the commission which was then in charge of the refugees, and the entire department, the head of the commission was Mr. Ljubisa Vladusic [phoen], Ljubisa Vladusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you write to them, the commission for refugees? What did you request and for what category of inmates?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wrote to them for prisoners of war and civilians because we received resources from the budget, that is to say from the Ministry of Finance. We were allocated funds from the budget for providing food to the convicted persons and those who were still under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that in addition to the main function during the war refugees of Muslim ethnicity were also accommodated in the Dom during the war. Is that the reason why you requested it from the commission for refugees because these people were refugees?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is already an associated exhibit, D3335.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm not familiar enough with my own case. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it was in different 65 ter number. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any other reasons apart from religious reasons for different cauldrons in which food was cooked for prisoners who were of different religious affiliations?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. We had established the practice for the Bajram and for the Serbian and Croatian Christmas, that on those days we would prepare special food. We called them reinforced meals with a cake and a glass of wine, and that was the practice in penal and correctional facilities then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 24 today, you were asked whether Avlijas was informed that the prisoners went to perform labour. Could you tell us whether Mr. Avlijas belonged to the civilian or military structures in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the assistant minister for the serving of sentences in the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were also asked whether he knew that prisoners went to perform labour. Did he have any authority or jurisdiction over the prisoners because prisoner and detainee, it's more or less one and the same word in English. Prisoner. But we should say prisoner of war or captive for the prisoners. Did he have any jurisdictions over POWs?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had jurisdiction over us. In fact, we called him boss or chief. He was the chief of the prison. He was our immediate superior from the civilian authorities. He was in charge of persons who had been convicted and who were under the jurisdiction of civilian courts. So that was the sole jurisdiction. The assistants had it, or rather, the Ministry of Justice, and of course we did as well, we who were the heads of the relevant institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the following: You said today that nothing was concealed. You were working for the state. In the name of the state, did you record every misdemeanour or violation or anything that the state had to know and had to prevent, or did you conceal anything, and how did Mr. Avlijas behave with regard to this?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992, we still have all the documents, all the records, every day, everything was recorded. A number of big notebooks and files, complete files with medical documents, consumption of food, everything was recorded as if there was no war at all. We recorded everything and registered everything as we used to do before the war. As I worked about this for 35 years, I worked only with convicted persons, and this aspect of the work is something I am completely familiar with, and we used this as our guidelines. And we applied this to all the other categories of persons who were at the KP Dom, who were accommodated there. POWs, civilians, whoever came to the KP Dom, we never concealed anything, whichever information the international instances or courts and this Tribunal requested, we always submitted everything. Nothing was secret. Everything has been recorded on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skiljevic. On page 10 and page 11, it was suggested to you that Rosic did not want to know about civilians, the late minister Rosic, the justice minister. Did you say that that was correct or that it was correct -- I'm sorry, perhaps I could quote to you what exactly was said on that particular page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then after that, a non-leading question should be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was the question at the end of page 10: [In English] "Are you stating there that you were, you informed the minister of justice of your concerns about civilians being held in the prison but he didn't want to discuss that; is that correct?" [Interpretation] And you answered: [In English] "That is correct. At meetings we also pointed out ...," [Interpretation] and so on and so forth. Was the reason that the justice minister did not inquire about these people was that they were civilians or because of who they were or because of who detained them and under whose jurisdiction they were?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That question shouldn't have been asked that way. The witness is given only two options. It should be asked in an open way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. Though this -- Ms. Gustafson's question was also misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But tell us why wasn't he interested in that category of the Dom's inmates?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice was not in charge of them. It didn't have the jurisdiction, and if as an organ the Ministry of Justice did not have the jurisdiction then the minister didn't either and that's why he acted in that way. What was the jurisdiction of the army, namely the POWs, and where the persons under investigation were under the jurisdiction of the military, that is to say the military courts, they were a category that was separate from those who were under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, and therefore he talked with us about those specific issues and not about the others which were not under our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what effect did it have, that they were civilians and he did not inquire about them?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not any effect. He talked with us, and we requested that these people should be transferred from the penal and correctional facilities because they only made trouble and difficulties for us, if I can put it that way. Because we had to take care about people who were staying with us and who were not under our jurisdiction, we had to provide them with a lot of care with respect to providing them with food and health service and satisfying all their other needs. That had to be seen to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 21, it is stated that at Zlatiste, some prisoners or POWs or captured persons were killed due to shelling. Can you tell us is there anything else in Zlatiste except the front line? Does this mean that they were at the front line?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there some kind of tower there? Is there any logistics, any depth?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the labour that was performed was always performed in the depth of territory, when they were doing something in the barracks after -- below Mojmilo Brdo. You cannot see the positions of the opposing sides there. You cannot see that from the tower at Zlatiste. You cannot even see the KP Dom or houses in Donji Kotorac or Novakovici. All that is above the combat lines. But in that area, in these locations, people were killed by shells and also by sniper fire. And as they were leaving, as they were going from the KP Dom to where they had to perform their labour between Kula and Lukavica in the location in Bijelo Polje on the road, as they were going and coming back, the same also happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about indirect mortar fire. What are the sections of Sarajevo, the city proper, and the general area of the city were those that could not be hit by mortar fire? That is to say where could you be and be sure that nothing would fall?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps Trtunici [phoen] up there, because in Kasindol where we were and where the hospital was, even there mortar shells sometimes landed. In Cilava [phoen] as well and in Pale, I mean, there was no great safety anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have served the army, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We just have to make pauses between question and answer, please. Can you tell me except for trenches was there anything else in the -- at the front line? You mentioned some communicating trenches. I'm not sure if it was properly understood what was meant by that. Are there any reserve positions or something else that is dug out and that is not necessarily at the front of the first front line, that is to say that is located in depth?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some communications or roads constructed to transport goods, and so on, because this area was not densely populated. Many refugees had arrived. Many facilities had been constructed but there were no access roads, access roads to the barracks, access roads to houses, access roads leading to hospital; that is to say whatever was needed so that these places could be reached as fast as possible and so that people could be removed from the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 18 you mentioned that people would drink when they went to perform labour. You mentioned the Serbian cemetery that was nearby and you said that not a single bottle of brandy had remained full. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what is the connection between a graveyard or a cemetery and brandy or rakia in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's close to the poultry farm where eggs were produced and the Serbian graveyard is there. According to Serbian customs, you leave some brandy at the cemetery after the burial is performed. So during the night, if it was there, after the work was performed, people would take the brandy and drink it because it was close to the buildings. And you had soldiers in the barracks who also consumed a lot of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it also a custom to leave something else in graveyards, such as food and so on, and did homeless people and who else -- or how did this all end up, the items which were left in the cemetery according to age-old customs?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly it was rakia or brandy that people were after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were told that some of the prisoners went to Grbavica. Was Grbavica a military location by its nature? Or what was it, in -- by its character, was it a military location or a civilian settlement?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, in Grbavica, there were -- I don't know the exact information, but I think it had about 10.000 residents who were living in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps if you know, do you know that in 1994, the international, or rather, the high commission established that out of the 10.000, 4.000 were Muslims? Did you know this?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about the following: You met Stanisic. You met Mandic. Did Mandic, when he arrived, to his premises, the premises of the ministry, did he come to his premises or offices or did he come to the prison?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mandic occasionally came to his own offices, and in these offices he held meetings because at the time this had been established. It was your duty. You had established the KP Doms and the courts, the lower court, the district court, were then set up in eastern Sarajevo and it was precisely on the premises of the KP Dom -- well, the premises. We are actually talking about the administration building, which belonged to the KP Dom throughout the war up until 1996, also housed the district court and the district public prosecutor's office. So it was a normal thing that the minister would hold meetings there with representatives of the Ministry of Justice. The assistants Vrljasovic [phoen], Avlijas, and others, they drafted certain regulations, being sure that they would maintain law and order and so on, and with his deputy at the time, that was Nenad Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to explain to the Chamber that if someone visits his offices or premises, is that within the complex and is administration building also located within the complex, or can you enter this building without entering the complex?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's next to the gate. It's at the gate itself and those who were staying there were at distance of about 70 metres, those who were convicted and those who were inmates and there were other facilities around those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also told that Minister Mico Stanisic, who was the minister of the interior, sometimes visited as well. Was the public security station in Kula also an integral part of the prison?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kula public security station was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Skiljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the KPD was closed down, when the convicts were released on the 6th of April, 1992, a certain time later a police station was placed there, the Kula police station. The former warden, Kreho, and the remaining staff of the KPD were also there, and some people from the farm, the Ekonomija. That was the situation until August 1992, when the police station moved to another building, also owned by the KPD at the same locality as the farm. And the station stayed there until 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In organisational terms was it part of the prison or did it belong to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They belonged to the MUP. We were parts of two different ministries: One was the Ministry of Justice, the other the Ministry of the Interior. The KPD was under the Ministry of Justice, whereas the police were under the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If Minister Stanisic was seen coming to the public security station, did he come to visit the prison or the police station?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He would visit his co-workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at P6277. You were asked how much earlier you learned that I was coming and Mr. Ashdown, and you said that you only learned of our arrival two hours in advance which was contested. Let's take a look at this document, P6277, page 26 through 28. Actually, the correct page number is 175, and I'm interested in lines 26 through 28. 175. Here is what you said then. I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Just that everything should be as normal and I practically found out about their arrival two hours before they would come because it was postponed and postponed all the time. First it was said that they would come at 1.00, then they didn't come at 1.00, so it was prolonged. I didn't even know if they would come at all." [Interpretation] In that interview, you said that you had learned of our arrival two hours in advance?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have page 180, lines 22 through 28. Here, we went through that fast: [In English] "And I think that minister was grateful."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. This passages never put to the witness in cross-examination, and now this is just a totally leading exercise for Dr. Karadzic to go to other parts and reads them out to the witness. If he wants to ask about things that are in this statement he should just ask the questions rather than reading out the witness's prior statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is nothing wrong with putting something to a witness and asking him whether it's accurate or not. The witness can say: No, this is wrong, or, yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, the witness started reading this paragraph but he was interrupted. I would like him to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what context he was stopped reading?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor interrupted him. The Prosecutor was not interested in that paragraph, Ms. Gustafson, that is. But I am interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of showing the passage, why could you not put the question first, some foundational question? Is it related to whether or not he was informed two hours before the -- their arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Excellency, I wanted to enable him to finish his answer. He started saying the minister said this and that. I can put the question differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see the question and answer first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to ask my question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in Serbian version which the witness had started reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you tell us, during this visit of the minister, what information did he get and how did he assess the work of you and your co-workers?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it was excellent. No remarks whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I seek to tender this page unless it is admitted already, but I believe part of it is admitted because Ms. Gustafson introduced something from this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And now it's for you to put this part to the witness. The witness didn't comment on this. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think the witness has given an answer that's basically the same as what's in his prior statement, so I don't see any reason for the statement to then be put to the witness. Normally that would only be to refresh recollection or impeachment. And I also don't see a basis for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all the same to me. I got an answer that the minister thought they were doing excellent work. With this page it would have been more complete, that he had commended them and that he enabled them to be in constant contact with him. I think this would have been a more useful to the Bench, but if you prefer otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skiljevic, I don't remember if I asked you in my examination-in-chief whether you were commended during your work or given any decoration or award.

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I was commended a number of times; those were penological commendations for my work. I also got oral commendations. I wasn't decorated, though, although I stood up before a tank and prevented them from shooting at the detention unit, because an order had been given to fire shells at everybody in the building. But I said, Only over my dead body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There have been suggestions today that the KPD was overcrowded, so can we get document P24237. Can we see page 3 in e-court, which is the second page of the document. Please focus on what it says about the other building -- persons of Croatian ethnicity while two Muslim women are in a separate room. All the dormitories have a sufficient number of beds, blankets, but there is a significant shortage of pillows, and so on, a TV set. And then they say further down, sanitary areas are operational, there is water, and the inmates were interviewed in the absence of the personnel. And the conclusion was that there were no objections. Although this report is not signed, is it in line with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything stated here is correct. I made some remarks to this report and it was signed by Professor Vukasin Gutovic. At the time he was the only inspector at the -- in the sentence implementation department. There was a shortage of electricity and water, but we made some furnaces in our workshops and we also received some from the ICRC, and all the dormitories had solid fuel furnaces. The 4th of July -- on the 4th of July, 1992, a shell completely destroyed the boiler room. That's why the only option for heating was fuel or solid fuel furnaces. This is how we provided for their needs. And since some of the areas are rather dirty, such as the pig farm or the poultry farm, and a generator had to work constantly, and therefore there were bathrooms where everybody could come and have a bath, though sometimes we would be without water, but then we went to a well and brought water in containers, to avoid epidemiological problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Has there been an epidemic?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see page 10, please. That's page 10 in the Serbian. Probably in the English too. It says here, the Kula catering facility -- it says 80 per cent of the window panes are destroyed. Further down it says damage by shrapnel, a part of the furniture stolen, so tell us how come these window panes were broken by shrapnel? Was the cafeteria targeted?

utterances.speaker: SONIBOJE SKILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cafeteria is some 250 or 300 metres away from the KPD. It is near the farm and it was badly damaged by mortar shells. Only in 1994, when there was the blue road running through the farm, which the civilians from Lukavica took to get to the airport, accompanied by international forces, UNPROFOR and SFOR, then there was no shelling after 1600 hours. After that, when the road was closed, the shelling would continue. Shells were fired from mortars. The facility was not in function, and only in mid-1994 was it used again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are some more things in that other interview but I won't deal with that because the interview has been admitted. Thank you for your evidence, Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Skiljevic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for being fair and all the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, I'd like to put this on the record. During the testimony of Dragomir Obradovic, the Chamber admitted 65 ter 1D7300 as Exhibit D3189. During his testimony a discussion ensued as to the correctness of the English translation of the first sentence in that document.
