The Chamber has asked for a revised translation of the document, and that the Chamber instructs the Registry to upload the revised translation onto e-court in replacement of the previous English one. The newly or the revised document reads -- I mean, the first sentence: At certain times 61 Muslims civilians were moved out of the village of Vrbanja instead of being removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kozic, please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kozic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Kozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation ] Good day, Mr. Kozic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask that you pause between my questions and your answers, and for us to speak our sentences out slowly without hurry so that everything could be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Of course. I also read the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D7720 in e-court, please. 1D7720.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the first page of this statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the last page to the witness now, please, so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully convey what you told the Defence team? Do you wish to change anything, clarify anything or amend anything?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in essence. Yes, if we go one item by item, perhaps there would be some things that I would change that are of a technical nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to ask you today in this courtroom the same questions, would your answers in essence be the same as the ones in this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes, entirely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this bundle pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are 15 associated exhibits and we would ask permission of six of them to be added to the Rule 65 ter list which they were not included as a result of inadvertence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just, I'm checking, the number I have is 14. Could you check the numbers again -- number again, whether it's 14 or 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've been at it a few times and I came up with 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fifteen. Let me hear from you first, Ms. McKenna. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning. I think I have 15 numbers as well, although I note that there are partial translations only of five of the documents. I presume that the Defence is only tendering those documents in part. And in relation to 65 ter 17311, there is no translation. I also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 17 -- I don't have that number. 17311 is being tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it's listed as an additional exhibit that's not being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My mistake, Your Honour. I'd also just like to query. The witness has said that he would make changes of a technical nature. I think this leaves some confusion on the record so perhaps Mr. Karadzic could clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Karadzic, you will take that up. Shall we go through one by one. The first one I have is 65 ter 5987. I take it that the Defence is tendering only the item that's dealt with, i.e. item 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about adding the cover page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, we could submit that to translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that understanding we will admit it. And next one, 5989, shall we do the same exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And same goes to the next item, 5994.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, these are actually Prosecution 65 ter numbers, so we will go ahead and submit them for translation and then give them to the Prosecution for upload unless they have the cover page translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there would be no problem with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The same goes for 5995. And next item the Chamber has is 17324. The Chamber does not see this as indispensable and inseparable part of the statement in that the witness did not participate in the delegation, he does not recall the report, and in any event I don't think he made any substantial comment on the report. So that will not be admitted. And the Chamber has no difficulty with the following numbers: 17457, 30231, 1D7897, 1D25775, 1D25776, 1D25778. And the Chamber has similar concern about 1D25779 to those in relation to 17324. So we will not admit this one for the similar reason. And the remaining two, 1D25783 and 1D25784 will be admitted. Is there any item I omitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think 1D25752 may have been omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What paragraph is dealing with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Fourteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Karadzic could kindly deal with it live in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I believe this document is already admitted as D3156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah-hah. That -- then it resolves everything. So shall we give the number for the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 65 ter 1D07220 will be D3364.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The remaining associated exhibits will be admitted and be given a number in due course by the Registry. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I would now like read the summary in English of Mr. Dusan Kozic's statement. [In English] Dusan Kozic was born in Ljubina on 8th of January [sic], 1958. He was an MP in the BH parliament from 1990 until 1992, and later a member of the Assembly of the Serbian People, and National Assembly of Republika Srpska. As national tensions grew and transferred to the assembly, the HDZ and SDA parties constantly disrupted the partnership agreed after the elections. The reconciliatory tones in the National Assembly were most often of Dr. Karadzic. Dusan Kozic became the prime minister of Republika Srpska from 18th of August, 1994, to 16th of October, 1995. The government was responsible to the National Assembly. Dusan Kozic found that the work of the government was independent from the Presidency. Dr. Radovan Karadzic neither carried out, ordered, supported, nor in any other way influenced the commission of war crimes against the non-Serb population in BH. Dr. Karadzic fully supported a decision of the government giving powers to the MUP and the Ministry of Justice and administration to collect information on crimes against humanity and international law relating to victims of all nationalities. Dusan Kozic and his colleagues worked hard to establish law and order in BH. He underwent efforts to make it impossible for any army or the police to abuse their positions, and to remove MUP employees that were overstepping their powers. The government made exceptional efforts to enable to -- independence of the judiciary. The formation of the SAOs were based on the laws of that time and were public. Alija Izetbegovic was informed and included in the negotiations. The role of the War Presidencies was to replace the Municipal Assemblies in order to make the work more efficient in the situations when we -- the assembly couldn't gather. They were informed that they must adhere to the decisions and guidelines regarding their work and any decision that impinged on the jurisdiction of the republican organs would be invalid. The government endeavoured to curb the self-will of the War Presidencies. A number of orders from various War Presidencies were suspended but the republican organs still had problems with establishing effective power in certain municipalities. In July 1995, a government delegation visited Srebrenica. Dusan Kozic recalls that the VRS demanded that the municipal secretariats for National Defence mobilise all available means of transport to evacuate Muslim citizens to Tuzla at their own request. The government did not have a prepared evacuation plan for the civilians from Srebrenica. In August 1995, Mr. Dusan Kozic attended a meeting between the political and military leaders of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republika Srpska. It was discussed that NATO and UNPROFOR were co-operating militarily with the B and H army by providing intelligence. At this meeting, Dr. Karadzic noted that future peace plans to be signed by negotiators must be shown to the Republika Srpska Assembly showing commitment to constitutionality and legality. The incident at Markale was also discussed. Generals Tolimir and Mladic were convinced that the shells did not arrive from the Serbian positions. Mr. Dusan Kozic was aware that there was a lack of co-operation between the civilian and military sector. On August the 22nd of 1995, Dr. Karadzic informed Dusan Kozic and his colleagues about conflicts between the military and state organs of the republic, which continued until the end of the war. [Interpretation] I have no questions for Mr. Kozic. I think that we can do without any additional documents, so at this point in time I'm not going to tender any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kozic, as you have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kozic. Now --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: -- just before we start I'd like to remind you that we are very limited in time, so I would appreciate if you could listen to my questions carefully and answer them as precisely and concisely as possible. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You were a founder member of the SDS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you were also a member of the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You were present at the constituting session of the assembly of the Serb people in BiH in -- on the 24th of October, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Could you please say that again? Would you repeat that question, the date of the event, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The 24th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: The forming of the Assembly of the Serbian People? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were awarded the order of Nemanjic by Karadzic's decree on the 9th of January, 1994, due to your role as a founder of the Serb Assembly and as a continuing member of the assembly. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, together with Nikola Koljevic, you accompanied Mr. Karadzic on his first visit to Slobodan Milosevic in September 1990, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And an UNPROFOR cable reporting on your appointment as prime minister stated, Kozic is known to be personally close and loyal to Karadzic - for the parties' reference that is D1164 - would you agree with this assessment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And Mr. Karadzic also showed loyalty to you throughout his -- throughout your career, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Indeed, after your resignation as prime minister - and for the parties reference this is P1417, English page 81, B/C/S page 101 - Mr. Karadzic stated: "I take this opportunity to once again single out Mr. Kozic as such example, model of hard working party member who subordinates all his intentions and plans to needs of state and people and party that appointed him. I want to thank him for our co-operation, although I believe that we will continue co-operating in future because Mr. Kozic remains our cadre and he will remain in one of important positions in the future." This statement reflects Mr. Karadzic's loyalty to you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I thank the president again. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 9 of your statement, you mention the reconciliatory tones used by Mr. Karadzic and Krajisnik in the National Assembly. Now, you, yourself, used language in the Bosnian Serb Assembly which could not be described as reconciliatory, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Well, you would need to refer me to it or quote. I don't think that I did, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's look at one such example.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further, I forgot that you raised the issue of some potential changes of a technical nature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Kozic left the possibility open, if we spotted something, but at that point he had not spotted any errors yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, what did you mean when you said that you would make changes of a technical nature with respect to your statement, Mr. Kozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2 of my statement, two letters were dropped in line 4 from the bottom. The sentence makes no sense. The word "kao," "as" was left out. Then in paragraph 4, this initiative was supported by all the deputies. I would add the word "nearly everyone" because three of our colleagues remained in the Muslim assembly. So this does not essentially have an effect on the whole, so we can just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 1 says that your birthday is 8th of December, but Mr. Karadzic read -- said in his summary that your birthday was 8th of January. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 8th of December is correct. I did hear that but I did not react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe I may have misspoke, I'm looking for P956.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kozic, these are the minutes of the 16th Assembly of the assembly of -- sorry, excuse me, 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in BH held on 12 May 1992. You'll see that on page 1, item 1 is the report on political conditions and the war in the Serbian Republic of BH to be presented by Radovan Karadzic. Now, during Mr. Karadzic's presentation, he set out the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serb people but I'd like to focus on what you said in this regard. And that's at English page 28 and B/C/S page 23. And you state -- regarding item 1, you said: "The situation in the Herzegovina theatre of operations is now good and the only objection we have is that too many weapons are being taken away." Then you continue: "And I have asked for the floor because of the following suggestion: The enemy, Ustashas and Mujahedin must be defeated by whatever means are necessary and only after that can we negotiate." Now, you'll agree, Mr. Kozic, that references to Ustashas and Mujahedin do not suggest a tolerance on your own part for the Croats and Muslims, do they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I don't see what else war would represent except suffering and tragedy for everyone, and the Ustashas and the Mujahedin are our enemies to this very day, so in the Balkans this is just general rhetoric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes the -- we could not hear the middle part of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] International law is still at war today with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kozic, the interpreter did not catch the entirety of your response. You stated: "I don't see what else war would represent except suffering and tragedy for everyone, and the Ustashas and the Mujahedin are our enemies to this very day, so in the Balkans this is just general rhetoric." Would you like to add anything to that response?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: My address at the assembly had to do with defeating the enemy. This is the goal of every war. Our enemies are referred to then as Ustashas and Mujahedin because both of them were present in the Herzegovina front. I still stand by what I said then because I believe that we needed to win the war in order to be able to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could look briefly at your acceptance speech on becoming prime minister, that's P1398, and that was -- while the document was coming up, I'll remind you this was the 44th session of the Republika Srpska Assembly on the 18th of August, 1994. And could we please have page 11 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S. And you will see that you state that: "For more than two years, the Serbian people is engaged in a superhuman struggle for its survival and freedom. The liberation struggle of the Serbian people and its heroic army have created and developed their state and showed to the enemy and the entire world that we shall not succumb to the Muslim Croatian plans to subjugate us and destroy our are national being. Great military victories have been achieved, Republika Srpska covers almost all its ethnic areas in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina." So again, your own language, upon taking position as prime minister, doesn't suggest a tolerance for Muslims or Croatians, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: You are wrong, Madam Prosecutor. Muslims and Croats who were our neighbours are not mentioned here. The Balkans were our common living space. We lived before and during the war, ones next to the others. I'm talking about military formations here. And there is no intolerance towards the people, but rather towards extremist military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different topic. Could we please have article -- or 65 ter number 17457. Now, this, Mr. Kozic, is the document that you discuss in paragraph 12 of your statement, and it's the article from "Javnost" paper, which you state that the -- the document will be coming on your screen in a moment but I'm just reminding you that this is the article -- or informing you that we are about to discuss the article which you say discusses alleged weapons smuggling that was uncovered thanks to you. And at paragraph 12 you state: "This is a journalistic explanation of the case and does not contradict the views of the SDS." Now I'd like you to just look at the top of that article where it states, "Information of the assembly of the eastern and old Herzegovina municipalities." Mr. Kozic, in fact, this is a reproduction of a statement made by SDS Main Board member Bozidar Vucurevic isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the articles. I do remember the events, but not this. But, of course, if you mean about what I said here, namely that the official authority representatives should not be involved in dirty games, this is still my opinion, or I share it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We will come on to discuss the substance of the article, but I just want to clarify its source. Could we please have 65 ter number 24920. I'm afraid we don't have an English translation of this article yet. If we could go to page 2 of this document -- well, actually, first, you'll note the cover page which states that this is a statement by Mr. Vucurevic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 of -- ah, I see we in fact do have an English translation. Could we please see page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, could we just read what this is? The subject, is it a statement or is it an announcement, a statement issued for the press? Because it's not a statement like a witness statement. It's a statement given for the press, and it's nicely translated here as announcement, because if we don't clarify that now it's going to create a lot of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it created much confusion. I think it's clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now if you could just review this statement by Mr. Vucurevic, can you confirm that this is the statement that was reproduced in the "Javnost" paper?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I cannot. The documents and the dates have to be compared. It is impossible to conclude just by looking at the screen to make a direct link. So I cannot from this point in time confirm this with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6284, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, turning to the substance of the statement, could we please see 65 ter number 11543.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, this you'll see, Mr. Kozic, is a report of the Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo, on the uncovering of smuggling of weapons into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and -- but as it states in the first line it relates to events which occurred during the night of 24th May 1991 in the Bileca municipality. I'd like to focus on the second paragraph, please, where it states: "At around 440 hours, a police patrol signalled a Javasta [phoen] freight vehicle which was coming from the direction of Niksic to stop. Since the vehicle did not stop at the patrol's signal, a police patrol was notified and it stopped and inspected the vehicle." If we could perhaps move to the second page in the English and if you review the next paragraph, it states that: "On checking the identity of the passengers, it was established that the vehicle was driven by its owner, Milutin Popovic, and that Dusan Kozic and Momcilo Tohojl were in the vehicle with him." If we can focus on the fourth paragraph of the document, it states: "While the driving documents were being checked, Dusan Kozic came out of the vehicle and presented himself as a member of the parliament of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He showed an MP's identity card and requested that immunity measures be applied towards him." Now, Mr. Kozic, you were released by the Bileca police immediately while the other people in the vehicle were taken into custody; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Neither were they taken into custody, nor was I released. We just came in front of the police station and when I noted that the police was multi-party or rather multi-ethnic, that there were both Serbs and Muslims among the policemen, I then left it to the police to do their job. I was afraid of abuse, namely that the policemen might be uni-ethnic and that the weapons would be sent on to Stolac and Mostar because the party position was that the arms were to be sent to the barracks. We had no need to do anything special. The arms were to be sent to the barracks. The police did their job. They conducted the on-site investigation. The weapons were handed over at the barracks in Bileca and the proceedings were completed before a court and it is now an adjudicated fact; namely, the judgement was passed. As I told you, both the people and the weapons ended up in the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's see what this contemporaneous document states about what happened on that evening. If we could focus on the next paragraph, which is the fifth paragraph, it states: "After establishing the identity of the persons, the patrol inspected the cargo platform and established that there were crates under the tarpaulin in which Kozic claimed wood was being transported. Since on Dusan Kozic's orders the driver refused to show the documentation and allow an inspection of the vehicle and cargo, the vehicle and persons in it were taken to Bileca public security station. And it notes that they found eight crates in the cargo section, each containing ten Russian-made automatic rifles and 16.800 bullets for these weapons." Mr. Kozic, rather than uncovering the smuggling, you were taking an active part in it, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I did not take an active part in it and I did not uncover it, but the police uncovered it which I said loud and clear. And the first part of what you said was meant to be a joke. I said wood because I didn't know the ethnicity, the ethnic composition of the patrol which stopped us. I requested we should go in front of the public security station, when I saw there were both Serbs and Muslims there, then I left it to them to do their work. I didn't even want to attend and stand there next to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I would just like to show the witness one more document on this topic, if I may have your indulgence, before the break. Could we please have 65 ter number 11544.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kozic, this is an article reporting a speech by Mr. Karadzic at an SDS press conference at which he commented on the transport of weapons from Bileca. And in the second paragraph, he's reported as saying that SDS claims that the weapons that were transported through Bileca were trophy weapons and it was only coincidence that the SDS deputy in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly, Dusan Kozic, found himself there. Now, Mr. Kozic, you'll agree that 80 automatic rifles and over -- almost 17.000 bullets couldn't be considered trophy weapons.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that neither then nor now did I know what was under the tarpaulin. And Dr. Karadzic was quite correct, I was there accidentally because the Serbian personnel from the MUP had the same information as the Muslim personnel and they reported that something was being smuggled. And you are now taking the whole event out of the context in which it took place. This took place at the moment when 50 trucks carrying weapons had entered Croatia from Hungary which was reported around the clock in the immediate in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and there was a stampede among the people. The wounds from the Second World War were opened again because there is not a single family there from which someone did not perish in Jasenovac or in one of the pits. We could not convince them that it was not necessary to go and try to find weapons but that they should rather respond to mobilisation call-ups in an orderly manner, or if they were not called up that they would report themselves to the staffs of Territorial Defence. And you have to hear this to the end because this moment is decisive for what I have to say. The SDS was building its -- the safety and security of the Yugoslav People's Army as the only legitimate military force. I learned about this event, and I went as the general manager of Soko, the socially owned enterprise, in front of these men. My official car with my driver drove in front of the truck. I didn't want them to be manipulated. And I'm telling you people were left to their own devices and trying to obtain any weapons they could find, those left from the Second World War or hunting rifles or they would buy it. It was a sort of psychosis that was widespread just before the outbreak of the war. And that was the context in which this event took place, and this, what I have just told, you is the correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6286, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.20. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kozic, I'd like to look at the letters that you refer to in paragraph 21 of your statement and which you describe in that paragraph as: "Documents which talk about my efforts as prime minister to maintain legality in the work and make it impossible for the army or the police to abuse its position of being an armed force."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 1D25783. I'm afraid I don't have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3368, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kozic, this is a letter from you to the Ministry of the Interior dated 15 February 1995. Stating that according to the VRS, on 13 February 1995, members of the Bijeljina public security centre confiscated 14 tonnes of fuel intended for the 35th Logistics Battalion of the VRS, and you in this document are ordering that this fuel be returned. And the second document that -- to which you refer in paragraph 21 is a fax of the same date, following up on this issue. Now, as prime minister, you were involved in the procurement of logistical support for the VRS, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Not only to the VRS but the VRS and the people in the republic as a whole. The main duty of the government was to supply the materiel for successful waging of war and also for the survival of the people under wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And this included during the period in which, according to your statement, there was a lack of co-operation between the military and the civilian sectors, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Do you have in mind this letter or -- I haven't really understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't receive interpretation of the witness's last --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last statement, Mr. Kozic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I asked you to repeat the question to me, and whether you had in mind the document which I have on the screen in front of me, or are you asking me a completely new question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: My question is simply whether you were involved in the procurement of logistical support for the VRS in the period during which you state that there was a lack of co-operation between the civilian and military authorities, that is summer and autumn of 1995.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I have clearly answered that question, that the main task of the government was to create all material and technical conditions for the people to survive in its territory and also for the waging of the war. So it wasn't only my task but the task of the government as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to look at some meetings that you held in connection with procurement for the VRS and other forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have P1473. And I'd like to see page 143 in the English and 145 in the B/C/S. Sorry, I appear to have the incorrect reference. If we could have -- move to page 306 of the English and page 310 of the B/C/S; and that's P1473.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kozic, this is a meeting with General Mladic and other VRS officers on the 17th of August, 1995, to discuss procurement. And again, according to your statement, this is a period in which there was a lack of co-operation or no co-operation between the military and the civilian sectors. And you'll see, if we move to -- at the bottom of that page in the English and continuing over you state that 100 rifles and 500 shells have been procured in Bulgaria. You discuss who paid for them and you discuss providing ammunition, money for ammunition, setting up a team to procure ammunition, and the procurement of ammunition from the -- or for the Herzegovina Corps from the Trebinje hydroelectric power station. So this evidence, doesn't it, very practical co-operation between the military and the civilian authorities in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Well, no, Madam Prosecutor. I stand by my statement that it was forced, unwilling, and depended on the situation on the ground. Of course, it did not imply a complete lack of communication. Everyone was doing his own job. It was difficult for us. We tried the best we could and the whole arrangement was made at the time when I had taken up my appointment in August 1995 [as interpreted] and Serbia had already imposed sanctions on Republika Srpska and we had already been under sanctions imposed by the European union, that is to say the rest of the world, and such an atmosphere necessitated that all factors in Republika Srpska make the maximum effort if we were to survive. So I don't really see what you want to achieve with this question. Of course, we were doing this. The ministry was doing its job. It had to supply the army and the people with what was needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify the transcript or the recorded that you took up your appointment in August 1995. It's correct that you took up your appointment in August of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: On the same topic, if we look at a similar meeting two days later, at page 308 of the English and 312 of the B/C/S, here, this is on the 19th of August, 1995, and here you're informing General Mladic that a group from Bulgaria will come and quote a price for the ammunition. And the group is coming with Branislav Lainovic, via whom the FRY is procuring ammunition. Now, Mr. Lainovic, to whom you referred at this meeting, was a leader of the Serbian Guard paramilitary unit and was also known for his activities as a participant in the illegal arms trade, the drugs trade and other criminal activities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I don't know, and I think not. Please show me the translation so I can see the whole text and then I try -- I can try to remember the whole event because I don't see the version in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The question -- the version in Serbian should be before you. My question is whether Mr. Lainovic to whom you refer --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I don't have the Serbian version. Oh, here it is. Could we scroll down on the Serbian version so I can see the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kozic, perhaps my question was unclear. My question is simply, in this document, you refer to Mr. Branislav Lainovic. My question for you is: This man was a known paramilitary and participant in the illegal arms trade, drugs trade and other criminal activities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with his CV. And secondly, he didn't even come there. I don't even remember this meeting. We never had any dealings with Mr. Lainovic, but we did with Bulgaria. Mr. Lainovic never came to Pale, nor did we meet to discuss this topic. And we did have some arrangements with Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at a document that relates to some more direct meetings that you had, and that's P6210. So, Mr. Kozic, this is an Eastern Bosnia Corps security department document dated the 20th of September, 1995. It's addressed to General Tolimir. And it states: "In the evening hours of 19 September 1995, at a working meeting of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly which was attended, among others, by Mr. Frenki and Bozovic, from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, and Zeljko Raznatovic, aka Arkan, on one side, and Mr. Kozic, the prime minister of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Boro Bozic, and organs of the authorities of the Bijeljina region on the other. It was allegedly agreed that Arkan and his units should take and liberate Teocak. This operation to liberate Teocak would be financed and paid for by the republican government, Kozic and Bozic, and it would cost 3 million Deutschmarks." Now, do you recall attending this meeting in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: The meeting never took place. I only know about Frenki from the media, and the same goes for Mr. Bozovic. I only met Zeljko Raznatovic once in passing in Banja Luka. I don't remember the date. The meeting didn't take place. I don't know these people, nor was this matter discussed. There wasn't even any intention to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kozic. I'd like to move on to a completely different topic. In paragraph 17 of your statement, you discuss P3115, which are the minutes of a government session held on the 24th of August, 1994. And in connection with that session, you state, in its work the government was indeed independent. President Karadzic attended the government session without participating in its work, only a few times, and out of respect. I'd like to read to you a statement that Mr. Karadzic made in connection with your predecessor, Mr. Lukic, and he made this statement at the 34th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly in August and September 1993 - and for the parties' reference, this is P1379, English page 255, B/C/S page 289 - and Mr. Karadzic stated: "Believe me, the government is mine. I am responsible for its functioning. I appoint and propose the government mandator. I have a brilliant relationship with Vlado Lukic. We are often together. He often comes to my cabinet. But I do not see the government. I attended government sessions twice. I am even entitled to be in the lead of the government to schedule sessions." So Mr. Karadzic is saying that while he doesn't attend many government sessions, he keeps a tight control of the government through Mr. Lukic. Was that your experience?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another statement by Mr. Karadzic, and this is 65 ter number 45416. And this, Mr. Kozic, is a short video from a talk show called "Open Programme" which is on Banja Luka TV and Mr. Karadzic is a guest on the show.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do we know the date of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We don't have a specific date for this, but it is clear from the context of the document that it is during the war. If I may have the Court's indulgence for a moment, we are just having some technical issues. I'll come back to the video, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Moving to an entirely different --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I have the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Perhaps we can simply look at the text of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So in this, Mr. Karadzic states: "At this moment we have a combination of a parliamentary and a presidential system. I have plenty of authority, even more than I exploit, and the parliament also has a lot of authority and that is where some unity has been achieved. Now I must tend to the government more because that is what the constitution allows me to do and requires me to do so that the unity of executive power is realised because we must control the executive power on a daily basis. We have to keep an eye on it daily." So in this interview, Mr. Karadzic speaks of controlling the executive power on a daily basis. This, again, suggests a tight control of the government by Mr. Karadzic, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: No. You are relying too much on media statements or articles from the papers, and taking that from the context in which these statements were made and with which intention, and that will lead you to wrong conclusions because some statements had a completely different purpose, to mobilise the people. I remember the debates during Lukic's government - Lukic was a great man by the way - that the government was rather static, and it wasn't up to the demands of the time. They were being too lenient. That's what I suppose the president meant. And when he says that he demanded fast, expeditious work, that was at a time of twofold sanctions. And now I can say - and now first apologise to Mr. Karadzic - something that few people in the RS know. On the 60th day of my term in office, I totally cut off the cash flow toward the president of the republic and replaced each and every dime under government control --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm going to interrupt you. Again I'm going to remind you of what I asked you at the start of your testimony which is to focus very specifically on the questions that I asked you and give answers that are as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: All right. So the answer to this question would be this statement was given for different motives. There was close co-operation, but certainly not under absolute control as the statement reads, at least not during my term in office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we think it can be admitted for context, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, again moving to a different topic, Mr. Kozic. At paragraph 24 of your statement, you state that you generally knew that operations were taking place to neutralise the Muslim army in the enclaves and that the government in Pale only had general information about fighting in Srebrenica. And you also state that the VRS demanded that the municipal secretariats for National Defence mobilise all their available means of transport in order to evacuate the Muslim civilians from Srebrenica. I'd just like to clarify on -- your evidence on this point. It's correct, isn't it, that the civilian authorities worked together with the military authorities in connection with the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: This is a -- there is an innuendo in your question, and it's wrong. We received information that many civilians had been gathered at Potocari and we used the resources of the surrounding municipalities and the economic operators to provide a means of transport to take the civilians elsewhere, but at the time we didn't even know where they would go or where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we are going to look at some documents which the civilian authorities received in connection with the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, if we could have P4528, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By "operation" what did you mean, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It is the witness -- by operation I mean the take-over operation and the evacuation of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kozic, this is a Ministry of Defence order dated the 12th of July, 1995, and it states, pursuant to a request by the Main Staff of the VRS dated 12th of July regarding the mobilisation of buses, and it's immediately mobilise all available buses from the municipalities of Zvornik, Visegrad, Vlasenica, Milici and Bratunac. Now, this document shows that the Ministry of Defence is mobilising buses at the request rather than the demand of the VRS, as you characterised it in your statement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: But I believe that my statement reads just the same, that the secretariat of the defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat and speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Kozic. Could you please repeat your response and speak a little slower for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I don't see a difference between the document on the screen and my statement which reads that the VRS requested from the municipal secretariat of national defence the mobilisation of all available means to evacuate the Muslim civilians who had expressed a wish to go to Tuzla, and that's what my report says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Kozic. It appears to be a translation issue with the English version of your statement. But staying with the issue of information that was available to the civilian authorities, could we please see P4935. Now, Mr. Kozic, this is a dispatch from the Zvornik public security centre to the Republika Srpska office of the minister of the interior, and it's dated 12th of July, 1995, and it provides detailed information in relation to the Hotel Fontana meeting and the action being taken following it. I'd just like focus on paragraph 5 or conclusion number 5, which is, I believe, on the next page in the B/C/S. And it states: "Acting upon the President Karadzic's order which was conveyed to us today over the phone, the 2nd Company of the Zvornik special separate police units shall be dispatched to Srebrenica with a task to secure all facilities of vital importance in the town at all costs and protect them from looting and misappropriation." And it states: "A platoon of this company will lie in ambush at Ravni Buljim since the Muslim groups were spotted fleeing along this axis." And just together with this document, I'd like us to look at P4942. Again, this is a document dated the next day, it's 13th July 1995, and it's from the Zvornik public security centre to -- reporting to the minister of the interior, and it states: "At the meeting with General Mladic this morning, we were informed that the VRS was continuing operations towards Zepa and leaving all other work to the MUP as follows." And there are a number of bullet points: The first is evacuation of the remaining civilian population from Srebrenica to Kladanj, about 15.000 by bus. Second, killing of about 8.000 Muslim soldiers whom we blocked in the woods near Konjevic Polje. Fighting is going on. This job is being done solely by MUP units, and the document continues. Now my question for you, Mr. Kozic, is: You agree that these documents are providing the minister of the interior, a member of your government, with very specific information in relation to what was going on in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: No. I don't agree. Please take into consideration that on the 11th I got my third child and I was often absent from the 11th of July until the end of my term in office. You are saying that this is co-ordinated but that's wrong. Information came in from various sides and the letter that we saw a short while ago, the one sent to the president, the government urgently replied and sent out a commission to make a snapshot of the situation so that we be informed of the state of affairs. All reports depending on their source had different connotations so we didn't have insight into the real situation. That is why we decided first to take care of the civilians, and to make possible regular life in Srebrenica by sending police there and we also sent a government delegation there to -- on a fact-finding mission. And we wanted to take care of the civilians. Certainly there wasn't -- there were no Serbs there. So we -- I wanted to take care of the Muslim civilians to see where they were from, Srebrenica, Bratunac, where they wanted to go. So what you see on the screen is the product of the personal knowledge of the author, because we all more or less got information from the media. What made our life difficult for three years and killed thousands of people now was resolved, liberated, and that is the content of this dispatch, and please don't take it out of its temporal context.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Just to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention in the transcript, line 9, page 79, this witness said "sending a commissioner and the police," the "commissioner" was omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Do you confirm that, Mr. Kozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I first said a commissioner and police, and a government delegation to write a report to create normal conditions for the protection of civilians and property.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And just to clarify, Mr. Kozic, in your statement it states that your third child was born on the 18th of July and then in the transcript -- then today you said that your child was born --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: No, it was on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: On the 11th, thank you. There is a number of documents in evidence which we don't have time to go through but which show that Mr. Karadzic was also receiving much information during or as the Srebrenica operations progressed - and for the parties' reference they are P2276, P4450, P5 -- excuse me, 3054 and P4463 - now, Mr. Karadzic, the minister of the interior and the minister of the defence were all members of the Supreme Command. You were also a member of the Supreme Command, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And yet your position is that, as prime minister, you had only very general information about what was going on in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You also state in paragraph 24 of your statement that the Muslim civilians asked on their own to be transported to Tuzla, and you talk about the fact that there was no prepared evacuation plan. You didn't know whether the civilians would wish to go or where they would go. Could we please see P2996. This is a dispatch of 12th of July, 1995, from the chief of the Zvornik public security centre, again to the office of the minister of the interior. And it states, at number 5: "A meeting will begin at 1000 hours with representatives of UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross and a Muslim representative from Srebrenica at which an agreement will be reached on the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj, a hundred trucks have been provided for transport." Now, Mr. Kozic, the meeting being referred to in this document was the third Hotel Fontana meeting between Mladic and representatives from Srebrenica's Muslim population following which the Muslim population was evacuated. So before that meeting took place, 100 trucks had already been provided to transport the civilian population out, in anticipation of the evacuation of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, could we zoom up para 5 and ask the witness to read out the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may collapse the English for the moment. Could you read the point 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At 10.00, a meeting with UNPROFOR and ICRC representatives begins and with the Muslim representative from Srebrenica, where agreement will be reached about the evacuation of all civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj, so that they may have more problems there. One hundred trucks for transportation have already been made available."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember we had a discussion about -- as to the translation of this sentence, whether the meeting has begun or will begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I wasn't aware of that discussion, but thank you for bringing that to my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, it appears on the basis of that translation that the meeting took place but -- excuse me, prior to the meeting taking place, 100 trucks had already been provided to evacuate civilians from Srebrenica. So my question for you is: This doesn't suggest that the civilians had any option to remain, does it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: It does not suggest what you're saying. You're persistently trying to get an affirmative answer to your assertion, whereas all the facts indicate that it is just the way he says, that there is confusion in the field, that some decisions must be made within half an hour by people who are there, officials there, and everything that I have said is proved by the documents that you are showing, the documentation, the sending of a team, the sending of the police to prevent robberies quickly, and so the responsible people had to reach decisions quickly in order to guard the civilians. And this is what I'm saying, that in these conversations we then found out what their wishes were. We did not make these up. It's a two-day whirl wind where all these decisions were brought, communication was conducted via telephones, Motorolas, and all of that, so I don't know why you would wish your conclusion to be the way it is, whereas everything in the documents indicates that it's quite the opposite. There was chaos and the civilian authorities are trying to introduce order as soon as possible because the care that I was talking about was not directed at the Serbs because all the Serbs were already dead by then and we could have lit candles for them, but it was directed at the Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 13758 on that topic. And I'm afraid we don't have a translation of this in your language but if I can explain that it is an UNPROFOR code cable from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan dated 14th of July 1995. If we look at the second page, point 6, it states, UNMO's report that they have been unable to sight any Bosnian civilians in Srebrenica. BSA troops have been sighted cleaning out the town by removing livestock, vehicles, household goods and other valuables. Karadzic has installed a civilian administrator in Srebrenica and the first Serb families have begun to move into the town. So, Mr. Kozic, it's clear from this document that contrary to your evidence, by the 14th of July, 1995, there were no Muslims left in Srebrenica but, rather, it was starting to be repopulated by Serbs. I should say no Muslims left in Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I don't believe in the authenticity of this letter. Perhaps this was written, but as I say, it does not reflect the truth in the field, on the ground. In three days, while the army was moving, only Serbs who survived and wanted to return could come in to see if their house was still intact. But as I say, I don't know. Until the 14th I was in Herzegovina and in the hospital in Podgorica, so I think that this passage does not reflect the actual state of affairs. There was nobody who could have returned there anyway. The government ordered that the town be cleansed in order to prevent disease from livestock and anything else that could harm the daily life of civilians, and in the documents, I looked at it, you have the report of a working group that confirms this, that the authorities were clearing the terrain, and preparing the town for civilian life to resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kozic on the same date, or on the 13th of July, 1995, the UN commissioners for refugees, Sadako Ogata, was reported as saying that the wholesale removal of Srebrenica's residents was one of the most blatant examples of ethnically motivated forced displacement we have seen yet in war. Is it your position that the entirety of Srebrenica's Muslim position -- or population freely chose to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Of course. They were probably frightened, tired, because of the three-year war, exhausted. And it was probably their wish to leave, and nobody asked them or made them leave. We expected them all to stay and we even expected people from Bratunac and the nearby municipalities to return, who had fled to Srebrenica before the war. But it's probably a result of fear and the wartime psychosis that they wanted to go to a safe place. So that report by Mrs. Sadako Ogata is not quite sincere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna as regards the date when the witness's third child was born, I checked, compared the two statements, and in the B/C/S it's noted as 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Yet again it's a translation issue obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware that I've reached the end of my allocated time. I just have one brief topic to deal with, if I may have your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kozic, again in your statement you spoke of the civilian authorities conflict with the military authorities and the tension between those authorities but the tensions that were heightened after the fall of the RSK and the loss of territories in western Republika Srpska. Now, this loss of territory was what led you to you tendering your resignation in October 1995; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: No. The main reason was the health problems of my child, that was number 1. Number 2, my colleagues from the Krajina asked that one of the three leading figures of Republika Srpska comes from the Krajina because the bulk of the population in the western part of Republika Srpska was that, and I believe that the request was legitimate, and I was already burdened by my family problems, and those two factors resulted in my resignation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Kozic, at the 54th Session of the Assembly, on the 15th and 16th of October 1995, there was extensive discussion of the loss of territory in western Republika Srpska, and who was to blame for it, and there were calls for the dismissal of certain VRS generals and also calls for your resignation. And Mr. Karadzic read out your statement, your letter of resignation which stated that due to a very complex situation in the western part of Republika Srpska, for matters of principle and political reasons, I hereby resign from the office of prime minister, and then you go on to make the point that you hope that they will nominate a man from the endangered areas of the western part of Republika Srpska and thereby strengthen their political position. So we agree that there was significant disagreement between the civilian and military authorities in relation to the events in the RSK and western Republika Srpska, but I would just like to focus finally on Mr. Karadzic's attitude to the Srebrenica operation as stated before the assembly, and in that same session where you resigned, which is P1415 for the parties' reference -- well, firstly, you'll be aware as a member of the Supreme Command that the take-over of Srebrenica was carried out pursuant to Directive 7 which was issued by Mr. Karadzic as Supreme Commander on the 8th of March, 1995. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I would need to look at the directive and read it first in order to be able to answer you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, let's see what Mr. Karadzic said at that session. He stated, at -- could we please see P1415. And could we have page 86 of the English and page 111 of the B/C/S. Just while the document is coming up, Mr. Kozic, at that session, at page 84 of the English and page 108 of the B/C/S, Mr. Karadzic says, "I have examined, approved and signed seven directives," and then we'll come on to what he says specifically about Srebrenica. This is page 86 of the English, yes. So halfway down that page, Mr. Karadzic states: "As the Supreme Commander I stood behind the plan for Zepa and Srebrenica, mainly for Srebrenica. Zepa was implied." And he continues: "I personally supervised the plan, without the knowledge of the General Staff, not even hiding anything, but I happened to run into General Krstic and advised him to go straight into town and pronounce the fall of Srebrenica and later we will chase the Turks around the woods. I approved an immediate task and a radical task, and I don't regret it." So, Mr. Kozic, at a time when the army's operations were coming up against fierce criticism, when the entire subject of that assembly was criticism of the army and what -- and its responsibility for its various operations, Mr. Karadzic took full responsibility for and staunchly defended the Srebrenica operation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the date of that assembly session, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: That assembly session was the 15th and 16th of October, 1995, and you may recall it as the session where there was a heated debate about the fall of the Krajina --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: And where was the session, in Banja Luka or in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have that information readily to hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says held in Banski Dvori in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall those words and that quote taken out of context. There were two shocks that we experienced. One was the fall of Srebrenica and the other the fall of the Krajina. So that the assembly dealt with those two major events in our history, and I really cannot state any particulars because I cannot -- I cannot remember anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall all the addresses and discussions by my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Perhaps it will assist your recollection if I tell you that at the 52nd Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, on the 6th of August, 1995, so after Operation Storm, Mr. Karadzic said, again on the topic of Srebrenica - and this is at page 111 and page -- of the English and page 94 of the B/C/S: "The time had come, and I signed Directive 7, to capture Teocak, Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde. The directive was signed and we embarked upon it." He states: "I was in favour of all the decisions we made and I support them all. All the decisions are recorded in the Supreme Command. I ordered in verbal and written form to attack Zepa and Srebrenica. There will be the right time to take Gorazde just as there was the right time to conquer Srebrenica." So once again, Mr. Kozic, I put it to you that Mr. Karadzic's position was to accept full responsibility for the military operation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: That is your assertion, but it is not mine. Simply speaking, I do not recall those words, nor can I give any comment on that, because I say again it was a confusing time where we had to reach decisions within a second that would be acceptable for the republic, for the people, for the prevailing situation around us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kozic. And thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. McKenna. Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, and I would like to start immediately, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kozic, are you able to tell us where the president -- the prime minister was from who replaced you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: From Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is that what you wanted to achieve with your resignation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: For a colleague of ours from the Krajina to succeed me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown a telegram by Ambassador Akashi of the 14th of July, about how there were no Muslim civilians in Srebrenica. On the 11th of July, did we know that the civilians from Srebrenica would leave, Muslim civilians from Srebrenica? Did we know that on the 11th of July? Did any of us know that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Well, this 11th of July is problematic for my personal reasons because I was in Podgorica for the surgery of my child then. So I can convey just comments which I learned of a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did any of your associates in the government seek on the 8th, 9th, 10th or 11th of July -- ask for buses and trucks for the evacuation of civilians?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Until the 11th, till 10.00 when this news arrived, and while I was still at Pale, this was not a request that came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then on the 12th, did the police from Zvornik inform that there would be a meeting at 10.00 at which a decision would be taken on where the civilians would decide to go? Were you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I -- I object to the leading nature of this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the document was shown, and it was read that a meeting would be held at 10.00. And my question is not about that document, but it's about whether it was the first meeting and whether there were any other meetings before that with the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, it's quite certain that I wasn't in Pale, so I cannot convey the comments that I got later from my colleagues with any certainty. Once I returned from Podgorica, these contacts were, and I don't know the exact date, were with representatives. I saw that broadcast on television. There were two or three prominent householders, hosts, from Srebrenica, but before that there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this Trial Chamber saw that there were two meetings prior to that on the 11th, at 8.00 in the -- at 11.00 and then at 8.00 in the evening. And for the transcript, Ms. McKenna describes those activities as an operation, even though the original order refers to that as combat actions and not as an operation, and this is important because the operation has to -- an operation has to be carried out by more than one corps. Well, you were asked today whether you as a member of the Supreme Command were saying that you didn't know something. Can you tell us whether, in July 1995, there were any meetings held of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that without any reminders on paper. This is for the mentioned family reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you don't know that there were any and you did not attend any; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That whole July and August period to me was a very confused time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was whether you attended any meeting in the month of July around Srebrenica or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when we are asking about the Supreme Command, can you tell us how frequent the Supreme Command meetings were, and what was most frequently discussed there? What was the most frequent concern --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection. This is beyond the scope of the cross-examination. The witness was simply asked whether he was a member of the Supreme Command. It doesn't open the door for Dr. Karadzic to discuss the Supreme Command generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the door was opened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question of this witness's knowledge, and how much he knew and where he got his information was called -- definitely put into issue by the cross-examination. I think this question is going directly to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Ms. McKenna, you asked the witness about the knowledge of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I asked the witness about his own knowledge in connection with the Srebrenica take-over. The question as to what the most frequent concern of the Supreme Command meeting was is entirely irrelevant to that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how frequently the meetings of the Supreme Command were held and what was discussed in these meetings which would then involve your knowledge of matters that you were summoned here for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: The meetings were not frequent. Most often the events on the ground were discussed, the present needs and requirements of the army, and the conditions that were prevalent during those particular days at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the role of the government in conducting the war and what were its responsibilities in terms of the army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: Just the provision of materiel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 73, you were told what I said about the government, and did I ever use these authorities stemming from the constitution to call a meeting of the government and to impose a certain agenda while you were prime minister?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 70 you said that you took over the post of prime minister in August 1994 and you said that Yugoslavia had already imposed its sanctions but the date was not recorded. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber when the sanctions of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia against Republika Srpska were imposed on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Kozic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was at the beginning of August, the 4th day of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Answering questions about weak co-operation or misunderstandings and tensions between the army and the civilian authorities, would you say that this related to supplies and provisions or to the degree of the control of the civilian government by the Ministry of Defence and others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOZIC
utterances.text: I was thinking about the degree of co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
